title: The Sanabrian Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Sanabrés
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.

spans.t: The Camino Sanabrés is a branch road. It leaves the Vía de la Plata at Granja de Moreruela, in the province of Zamora, turns west into the Sanabria mountains, crosses into Galicia above A Gudiña, passes through the thermal city of Ourense and comes into Santiago de Compostela over the River Sar. It is ~370 km in all, this book walks it in sixteen days, and it is a road that asks you to plan.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this quiet road is your Camino, what each of its sixteen walking days asks of you, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days by region, and the chapter on the long days, which shows where they can be split. If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way".
If you are walking the Vía de la Plata from Seville, this book is your last stretch. It begins where the two roads part.
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly, more so on a road with few pilgrims and long gaps between villages. For those answers, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
Every distance here carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate. Where something depends on the season (snow, fog, heat, a flooded path), the book says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way. Each stamp is a
sello
. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules, which the chapter on arriving sets out. The
Xunta
is the regional government of Galicia, and the
Junta
that of Castilla y León, the region of Zamora. Both publish guides that this book uses.
Place names follow the official pages: Spanish in Zamora, Galician from the border (A Gudiña, Laza, Ourense). Older Spanish sources write Orense, La Gudiña and Vilar del Barrio for the same places.
Carry what you need, plan your nights ahead, and take your time over the high pass.
Buen Camino.
Where it goes

The Camino Sanabrés starts at Granja de Moreruela, a village in the province of Zamora, in Castilla y León, on the Vía de la Plata. The Zamora tourism board writes that behind the village church you take the direction marked Ourense, saying goodbye to the Vía de la Plata, which goes on towards Astorga. It adds that for most walkers the pilgrimage does not begin here: it continues.

From there the road crosses the River Esla, follows the valleys of Valverde and the Tera, climbs into the mountains of Sanabria to Puebla de Sanabria, and crosses the Padornelo pass to Lubián, the last village in Castilla y León. It enters Galicia near A Canda, in the province of Ourense, goes by A Gudiña, Laza and Vilar de Barrio to the city of Ourense, and then by Cea and Dozón to Lalín, in the province of Pontevedra. At A Laxe, in the parish of Bendoiro, the Camino de Invierno joins it, and the two roads go on together over the River Ulla, where you enter the province of A Coruña, to Santiago.
Which road is this?
The official pages do not agree on its name.

items.t: The Xunta de Galicia calls it the Vía de la Plata or Camino Mozárabe, and its pages on the road never use the word
Sanabrés
The Junta de Castilla y León calls it the Camino Mozárabe-Sanabrés.
The Confraternity of St James calls it the Camino Sanabrés.
The CaminoPlus catalog calls it the Camino Sanabres.

spans.t: It is one road.
Sanabrés
means "of Sanabria", the mountain district around Puebla de Sanabria.

The Vía de la Plata is a different and much longer road. The CaminoPlus catalog lists it from Seville, at ~1,000 km, and the Confraternity says walkers take six to eight weeks. The Xunta says its name has nothing to do with silver: it comes from an Arabic word for a wide paved road. This book covers only the part the Sanabrés follows from Granja de Moreruela, and the app has the Vía de la Plata as its own route.
How long is it, and how many days?

The app's catalog gives this road a start and an end but no distance and no number of stages. The CaminoPlus website lists it as ~370 km and 15 to 17 stages. The official sources agree once you add their parts together.

items.t: The Junta's guide, in an edition of 2010 updated in 2011, gives ~373 km from Granja de Moreruela to Santiago, ~149 km of them to Lubián.
The Xunta gives the part it describes as ~222 km by Laza and ~253 km by the longer way through Verín. Its first stage is titled Lubián to A Gudiña.
The Junta's figure to Lubián and the Xunta's length by Laza make ~372 km. The sixteen days of this book add up to the same.

spans.t: Stage counts vary. The Zamora tourism board suggested eight stages from Granja de Moreruela to A Gudiña in a leaflet of 2010, and the Xunta lists nine in Galicia by Laza, starting with Lubián to A Gudiña. Together, without counting that one twice, they make sixteen. This book names each day by those stage towns, and the chapter on the long days shows where a day can be split. Plan on ~370 to ~375 km.
Why it exists

The Junta's guide says this was not a Jacobean road in origin. It grew out of a link between the old kingdoms of León and Galicia, and the royal chronicles show kings on it: Alfonso IX in the spring of 1225, and in 1506 Philip the Handsome, who met Ferdinand the Catholic at Remesal after travelling from Santiago to Ourense and Puebla de Sanabria. The guide cites a pilgrim's account of the middle of the eighteenth century, and names pilgrims' hospitals at Santa Marta de Tera, Rionegro del Puente, Verín, Monterrei and Ourense.

The Xunta tells it from the pilgrim's side. In the second half of the thirteenth century, after the Christian conquest of Córdoba and Seville, it says, pilgrims from Andalucía and Extremadura began to use the Vía de la Plata. Some went on to Astorga and joined the Camino Francés. Others took the diversion by Puebla de Sanabria and A Gudiña, and went by Laza or Verín to Ourense and Santiago. The Zamora tourism board says walkers took it to shorten the road.

The modern road is a revival. The Junta's guide, in 2010, says volunteers and Jacobean associations recovered it, and that it had lately gained attention. So it is an old way, with an uncertain pilgrim pedigree, and a young life as a Camino.
What it feels like

The Zamora tourism board describes country that changes by the day: Castilian plain, rolling land around Tábara, the valleys of Valverde and the Tera, the most fertile in the province, and then the mountains of Sanabria, a landscape you do not leave until the Apostle's tomb. The Junta's guide says the road lacks the crowding of the older, more traditional roads, and invites a slow walk. The Confraternity says you can expect a relatively quiet and peaceful arrival in Santiago.

Quiet does not mean silent. The Junta says the old natural entrance to Galicia, the Portillas, was bypassed when new roads, the Rías Baixas motorway among them, took a straight line. Several of the Xunta's stage pages put the national road N-525 beside the path, and the Zamora board's leaflet counts the crossings of the motorway. You will cross them and walk beside them.
How hard is it?

The app's catalog rates the Camino Sanabrés 3 on a scale of 1 to 5, the same as the Camino Francés and one below the Camino Primitivo. The app's own note for the road says services are thin, so confirm lodging.

The Xunta rates the road in Galicia Medium. It gives its first stage, Lubián to A Gudiña, and its last, into Santiago, a Low, and the seven between a Medium. It marks two sections of the stage from A Gudiña to Laza as High. This book's sixteen days average ~23 km, but three of them are ~34 km or more.

The sources disagree about services. The Junta's guide, in 2010, says the road has enough hostels and services to be entirely workable. The Confraternity of St James, writing about the Vía de la Plata and its Sanabrés branch, says that road is hard because of the lack, or unreliability, of stops for rest and food, and asks for extra care in planning the next day's stage. Both can be true on one road. Plan, then confirm.
Who it suits

items.t: Walkers who want quiet, and a long view with few people in it.
Walkers who like to plan: your nights first, then your days.
Walkers who are fit for a ~30 km day, or who will use the split points in the chapter on the long days.
People who enjoy changing country: a plain, a river valley, a pass at ~1,260 m, a city of hot springs, and the green hills of the Deza.
Those who have walked the Vía de la Plata from Seville and are turning towards Santiago.

spans.t: Who might choose another

items.t: A first Camino walker who wants company and a bar in every village may be happier on a busier road. The Confraternity says the road is gaining in popularity as an alternative to the busier Caminos, and that you can expect solitude if you want it, with plenty of company where you sleep.
If sixteen days is too many, you can walk only the end. The last ~107 km begin at Ourense, and the chapter on arriving looks at what that means for the Compostela.
If you dislike road walking, know that the Way runs beside the national road N-525 and crosses the motorway more than once.
If you cannot walk in heat, avoid July and August on the Zamora plain.

spans.t: How it compares

It is longer than the Camino de Invierno, which is ~260 km and joins this road at A Laxe, ~50 km from Santiago, and far shorter than the Vía de la Plata, which starts in Seville. Wikipedia, citing the Pilgrim's Office, says that of the compostelas granted in 2013 the Vía de la Plata had 4.2 percent and the Camino Francés 70.3 percent. That is an old figure for the whole of the Plata, not this branch, but it shows the scale. The Camino Francés and the Camino de Invierno have their own books in this series.
Language
Spanish will serve you in Zamora and most of Galicia. The Xunta's pages write place names in Galician, so expect
rúa
ponte
and
camiño
, "street", "bridge" and "way".
The short answer

The app's note for the road says the best time is April to June, and September. The Confraternity of St James, writing about the Vía de la Plata and its Sanabrés branch, points the same way: set off between the early spring rains and well before the heat of early summer, or come in autumn once the summer heat has gone. Summer temperatures, it says, can pass 40 degrees and should definitely be avoided.
These are patterns, not forecasts. For the week you walk, read the warnings of AEMET, the Spanish state weather agency.
Two climates on one road
The road starts on a high plain and ends in the wet north-west, so the weather changes with the days.

Zamora, on the plain at ~650 m, stands in for the first part. By Wikipedia's table, which draws on AEMET's records for 1991 to 2022, the mean daily high is ~9 °C in January, ~18 °C in April, ~22 °C in May, ~28 °C in June, ~31 °C in July and ~26 °C in September. The record is ~41.8 °C, set on 14 July 2022. Nights in January average ~1 °C, and Wikipedia says fog is common in winter. Rain is light: ~12 mm in July, ~55 mm in October.

Ourense, on the Miño, is hotter in summer and wetter in winter. The mean daily high is ~31 °C in July and August, and Wikipedia's table gives a record of ~44 °C in July. October rain is ~119 mm. Santiago, at the end, is wetter again, with ~214 mm in October and ~196 mm in January, and only ~31 mm in July.

Between the two lies the mountain. The road climbs to ~1,260 m at Padornelo, and the Xunta describes stretches above a thousand metres in the Serra Seca. The Junta's guide says that even in summer, in the last villages of Castilla y León and across Galicia, you can expect a fall in temperature, fog and the risk of rain in any season.
Month by month

items.t: April and May.
Cool mornings on the plain, wetter in Galicia. About 13 hours of daylight in mid-April. The Confraternity likes this season for the flowers and the long days.
June.
Warm on the plain, ~28 °C at Zamora, with about 15 hours of light at midsummer. Start early.
July and August.
The hot months. Walk at first light, plan to end by early afternoon, and think twice about the Zamora days.
September.
Still warm, ~26 °C at Zamora and ~28 °C at Ourense, with the rain coming back to Galicia.
October.
Mild and wetter. About 11 hours of daylight in mid-October. Check the sunset time for the week you walk.
November to March.

Short days, about 9 hours of light at midwinter, with fog on the plain and, the Xunta says, frequent snow in the hardest months on the high ground, even at ~736 m on the road to Bendoiro. Check what is open before you plan a night, and keep a way to stop early.

spans.t: Daylight

These daylight figures are this book's own calculation from the sun's position at Puebla de Sanabria and Ourense, and the two places agree: about 9 hours at the December solstice, with sunrise close to nine in the morning, and about 15 at the June solstice. The Xunta advises walking only in daylight, not before dawn or after sunset.
The Holy Year
2027 is a Jacobean Holy Year, because 25 July falls on a Sunday. The Holy Door of the cathedral is opened only in a Holy Year. You may find Santiago busier, so ask early about the way home.
The credencial

The credencial is the pilgrim's passport, a folded card of stamps. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says it identifies the pilgrim, gives access to the hostels of the Way, and is the proof you show when you ask for the Compostela. It is issued, the Office says, by a parish church, a confraternity, a diocese, an association of friends of the Way, or another Christian institution connected with the pilgrimage. The Office's pages list confraternities and associations in Spain and worldwide, so start there. If you are coming off the Vía de la Plata, you will already have one.

Stamps are normally collected where pilgrims sleep, but the Office says you can also get them at parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. On a road with long gaps, remember that list. The Office also mentions a digital credential, an app. Read the Office's page before you rely on one.
Getting to Granja de Moreruela, and home from Santiago

Granja de Moreruela is a village: the Junta's guide counts 313 people, and Wikipedia 337 in a census of 2004. The sources read for this book say nothing about public transport to the village. The nearest city is Zamora, and Wikipedia says Zamora has a railway station on a high-speed line and a bus station with services to nearby villages and larger cities. Ask in Zamora about the connection and check it in the month you travel, because timetables change. The Zamora board's leaflet of 2010 gave Zamora to Granja de Moreruela as two stages, so you may prefer to walk in.

Ourense has a railway station, which Wikipedia places in a western suburb, across the Miño from the main town. Santiago's airport is ~12 km east of the city, and the city has a railway station. Do not plan a tight connection for the day you arrive: you will want to see the Pilgrim's Office and the cathedral first.
Training

The Xunta's advice is to start training some months before, with walks that grow gradually in time and difficulty, and to plan the stages to suit what you can do. "The Camino is not a race", it says. It also asks for steady warm-up and stretching on the way, with attention to the calves.

On this road that advice has teeth, because three days are ~34 km or more and the high ground comes in the middle. In the weeks before you leave, practise ~20 km on two or three days in a row with the pack you will carry, and a longer day of ~30 km. Include hills, downhill as well as up: your knees and toes will feel the descents.
What to carry

The Xunta's advice is plain. Keep the pack to what is essential, and never above 10 kg. Wear boots or shoes you have already worn, and the Xunta prefers trekking or mountain boots with a hard sole, with sandals for the evenings. Wear well-fitting socks, cotton and seamless in the Xunta's advice, with a second pair of wool socks if you wear boots, and keep them clean. Its small first-aid kit has what you need for your feet and skin: needles, gel dressings, plasters, bandages, small scissors, sun cream and moisturiser. It asks for about two litres of water a day.

Add what this road needs. The plain and the Galician descents are sunny, so carry a hat and sun cream. The mountains can be cold and wet in any season, so carry a warm layer and a waterproof that covers the pack.
Money, language and maps

Carry some cash as well as a card, and do not assume that a small place will take cards: ask. Spanish will serve you; in Galicia, place names on the Xunta's pages are in Galician, which is close to Spanish.

Save an offline map before you leave home. The Confraternity says the Vía de la Plata is generally well signed with yellow arrows, but the Zamora board's leaflet of 2010 noted poor waymarking at a few points, and waymarks change. The Xunta's route page offers a KML file of the way, a format many map apps can read. The CaminoPlus app is built to work without signal. It is still in development, and what it holds for this road is described at the end of this book.
Booking ahead

The app's own note for this road says services are thin, so plan your nights ahead. In Galicia the Xunta's public hostels take no reservations, so for a bed there you simply arrive. For any other place, ask in the app, and phone or message the day before.

chapters.title: Zamora: Granja de Moreruela to Rionegro del Puente

spans.t: The character of these days

Three days cross the open country of Zamora, from the Esla to the valley of the Tera: farmland and holm-oak scrub, wide tracks, long straights, and villages of stone, adobe and slate. The stages are the Zamora tourism board's own suggestions, and the distances come from the Junta de Castilla y León's table. Both publications are from 2010 and 2011. The churches and the landscape will be the same. Waymarks, surfaces and services may not be, so check before you go.
Day 1: Granja de Moreruela to Tábara (~26 km)

You leave the Vía de la Plata behind the village church, following the arrows for Ourense. Wikipedia says the abbey of Moreruela, in the same municipality and from the twelfth century, is often claimed as the first monastery of the Cistercian Order in Spain. Then comes a day of wide tracks across farmland and a descent to the Esla, which you cross by the Quintos bridge: nine stone arches, more than a hundred metres long, built in 1920, the Junta says.

After the river you climb to Faramontanos de Tábara, whose church of San Martín dates, the Junta says, from the thirteenth century. Tábara has a Romanesque church of Santa María, consecrated in 1132, the Junta says. It adds that the Sierra de la Culebra, a regional reserve, is close, and that eagles, wolves and deer live around the town. The poet León Felipe lived in Tábara as a small child, and the Junta's guide prints one of his poems about the pilgrim who always takes new roads.
The Zamora board describes long open tracks, so take water and sun protection. The Junta's table gives ~26 km and the Zamora board ~28 km.
Day 2: Tábara to Santa Marta de Tera (~23 km)

The day follows the quiet valleys of Valverde and the Tera, past Bercianos de Valverde, Villanueva de las Peras and Santa Croya de Tera. The Zamora board calls the land near Bercianos beautiful: holm-oak hills with rock-rose.

Santa Marta de Tera is the reason to walk this day slowly. The Junta dates its Romanesque church to 1077, on the site of a monastery that, it says, King Ferdinand and Queen Sancha gave to the diocese of Astorga in 1063. On the south portal is St James as a pilgrim, with a bag marked with a scallop shell and a staff in his right hand, and his left hand raised, palm open, in greeting. The Junta calls the carving a symbol of this branch of the Vía de la Plata, and the Zamora board calls it the oldest sculpture of the pilgrim St James. The Junta adds that twice a year, on 21 March and 22 September, the morning sun enters the church by a round window and lights one capital.
The Junta's table gives ~23 km. The Zamora board's leaflet, which goes round by Pueblica de Valverde, gives ~27 km.
Day 3: Santa Marta de Tera to Rionegro del Puente (~27 km)

The Tera is your companion for most of the day, through Camarzana de Tera, Calzadilla de Tera, Olleros de Tera and Villar de Farfón. At Camarzana the Junta says a late Roman villa came to light in 1861, with mosaics. Calzadilla's name recalls the Roman road number 17 of the Antonine Itinerary, between Braga and Astorga. At Villar de Farfón, the Junta says, the lands of Sanabria begin, and a reservoir drowned the old mills.

Rionegro del Puente lies in the Carballeda district. Its brotherhood, the Cofradía de los Falifos, was probably founded in the Middle Ages, the Junta says, and its main aim was to welcome pilgrims. It also cared for the sick and for foundlings, and repaired roads and bridges: some documents speak of thirty-five bridges, a figure the Junta admits may seem exaggerated, though one document states it plainly. The village was also the home of Diego de Losada, founder of Caracas.
The Junta's table gives ~27 km and the Zamora board ~23 km. Both end the stage at Rionegro del Puente. The villages that follow are very small, so settle your bed the day before.

chapters.title: Sanabria: Rionegro del Puente to Lubián

spans.t: The character of these days

Four days take you up into the mountains. The Junta's table puts Rionegro del Puente at ~810 m, Puebla de Sanabria at ~960 m and the village of Padornelo at ~1,260 m. Holm oak gives way to oak, chestnut and heather, and the houses turn to granite and slate. The villages are small, some of them tiny, and between them run the national road N-525 and the Rías Baixas motorway, which the path crosses several times. The sources are the same as before: the Junta's guide and the Zamora board's leaflet, from 2010 and 2011.
Day 4: Rionegro del Puente to San Salvador de Palazuelo (~19 km)

This is a day of small places. Mombuey comes first, ~8.5 km out. The Junta says the Templars held the church there, and that its slender Romanesque tower of the thirteenth century has a defensive look the Order is credited with. It calls the tower a landmark for pilgrims.

Beyond lies Valdemerilla, with twelve inhabitants, and an inscription that the chapter on the inner Way quotes. Then come Cernadilla and its reservoir, and San Salvador de Palazuelo, a village strung out along the road in the old Jacobean way. The Zamora board praises the granite markers carved with scallop shells that the council of Cernadilla set up. Both sources give ~19 km. These places are small, so check that the village you want for the night can house you.
Day 5: San Salvador de Palazuelo to Puebla de Sanabria (~22 km)
The day passes Entrepeñas, Asturianos, Palacios de Sanabria, Remesal, Otero de Sanabria and Triufé. At Entrepeñas the Junta says chestnut trees begin to predominate, and the villages hold a
magosto

, a feast of chestnuts. At Asturianos it singles out two walnut trees centuries old. At Remesal a hermitage dated 1506 recalls, the Junta says, the meeting of Ferdinand the Catholic and Philip the Handsome. At Otero de Sanabria stands the sanctuary of Our Lady of the Remedies, patron of Sanabria.

Puebla de Sanabria is the most important place on the road, the Junta says. The town stands on a hill between the Tera and the Castro, and is declared a historic ensemble. It has a granite castle of the Counts of Benavente from the middle of the fifteenth century, walls of the twelfth and thirteenth, and the Romanesque church of Santa María del Azogue. The Junta says Puebla once had its own hospital for pilgrims. Both sources give ~22 km, and the Zamora board calls it a marathon day.
Day 6: Puebla de Sanabria to Requejo (~12 km)

The shortest of the mountain days, and a good one to take slowly. The Zamora board gave two ways out of Puebla: along the River Castro, or by Lobeznos and Pedralba de la Pradería. Both reach Terroso, which the Junta calls a Jacobean place above all others. Its church of Santiago has scallop shells carved on its door nineteen times, and a text beside the church says that welcome is Terroso's history.

Requejo stands at the foot of the Padornelo pass. Near it, the Junta says, runs the trail of El Tejedelo, more than five kilometres long, through a mixed forest of 139 hectares with one of the most important populations of yew trees in the Iberian Peninsula. Near Puebla lies the glacial lake of Sanabria, a natural park since 1978, which the Junta says is one of the few glacial lakes of the Iberian Peninsula. It is off the Way, so keep it for a rest day. The Junta's table gives ~12 km and the Zamora board ~12.5 km.
Day 7: Requejo to Lubián (~19 km)

The Padornelo pass is one of the high points of the road: the village of Padornelo stands at ~1,260 m by the Junta's table, and the Xunta puts the next pass, Portela da Canda, at ~1,262 m. The Junta's entry for Padornelo mentions a stone cross with inscriptions at the top of the Portilla pass, where the border between the kingdoms of Galicia and Castile once ran. The Zamora board gave two ways up, a path and the old national road, and the path may not be as it was in 2010. Ask in Requejo, and cross the pass only in good weather.

After the pass you come down by Padornelo and Aciberos to Lubián, ~1,024 m, the last village of the Camino Sanabrés in Castilla y León. The Junta says that here you meet the first of more than a hundred sculpted stones, each one different, made by the Ourense sculptor Carballo, which stand along the road in the province of Ourense. Three kilometres from the village it lists the Celtic hillfort of As Muradellas, from about the third century BC.
The Junta's table gives ~19 km and the Zamora board ~23 km.
The character of these days

Four days take you over the border and across the high country of Ourense to the city of hot springs. From here the figures are the Xunta's, from its stage pages for the Vía de la Plata by Laza, which this book follows in the Spanish originals, because the Xunta's English pages can be machine-translated. The Xunta rates the days Low, Medium, Medium and Medium. The Junta's table, from 2011, differs by a kilometre or two, and by ~3 km on the first day. Each day says so.

The Xunta says the road enters Galicia at the pass of Portela da Canda, ~1,262 m, in the municipality of A Mezquita. It calls A Mezquita a historic meeting point of the people of Castile, Galicia and Portugal, a land crossed by pilgrims, but also by reapers, muleteers, dealers and travellers.
Day 8: Lubián to A Gudiña (~27 km)

The Xunta's page for this stage is titled Lubián to A Gudiña, and its description begins at the pass. It rates the stage Low, though all three of its sections are Medium-High. From A Canda you reach A Vilavella, whose church is dedicated to Santa María de la Cabeza, and then go down by a bridge over a stream and old paved ways between centuries-old stone walls, to O Pereiro. The Xunta calls this a land of great stonemasons. Then you come into O Canizo, ~1,067 m, beside the N-525, and on to A Gudiña.

A Gudiña, the Xunta says, was famous from the eighteenth century for its traffic and its inns for pilgrims and travellers. On 15 July 1506, it adds, Queen Joanna and her husband Philip the Handsome stopped here, the same year, by the Junta's account, that Philip met Ferdinand at Remesal. The Xunta gives ~27 km, the Junta's table ~24 km and the Zamora board ~23 km. Start early.
Day 9: A Gudiña to Laza (~35 km)

This is the hardest day of the road and the first to plan with care. The Xunta calls the way the Verea Vella, or Verea Sur, and says that in the sixteenth century it was called the Camino Francés and the Camino Real. It crosses the Serra Seca, landscape above a thousand metres, where the Alto de Picaños is ~1,104 m. You pass A Venda do Espiño, A Venda da Teresa, A Venda da Capela and A Venda do Bolaño. A
venda
is an inn, and the Xunta describes this as land of half-abandoned villages. The reservoir of As Portas lies to the right, and the natural park of O Invernadeiro to the north.

The Xunta rates the day Medium, and its first two sections, from A Gudiña to Campobecerros (~21 km) and from there to Porto Camba (~3 km), High. After Portocamba you go through a mountain valley of the Serra de San Mamede, by As Eiras, into Laza, which the Xunta and the Junta both say is famous for its carnival.

Campobecerros, ~21 km in and ~15 km short of Laza, is the natural place to split the day, but ask whether you can sleep there. The Xunta gives ~35.5 km and the Junta ~34.4 km. Carry food and water for the whole day. Do not trust a village on the map.
Day 10: Laza to Vilar de Barrio (~19 km)

A shorter day after a long one, and it climbs. The Xunta says you go up the valley of the River Támega by Soutelo Verde and Tamicelas, then climb steeply to A Alberguería, where there was an inn for travellers and a charity hospital for pilgrims. Beyond lies high heathland, short of trees, with the colours of heather, and a sharp climb below the Alto de Paradiña and Monte Talariño.

At Sarreaus, the Xunta says, the River Limia rises, the river the Greeks called Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, which the Roman general Decimus Junius Brutus crossed. Vilar de Barrio is the head of a municipality in A Limia, a broad district at the centre of the province of Ourense. The Xunta gives ~19 km and the Junta ~20 km.
Day 11: Vilar de Barrio to Ourense (~35 km)

Another long day, on a wide, comfortable way. The Xunta says that from Vilar de Gomareite it is called the Verea de Santiago, with stone paving and stretches that are sometimes flooded in winter and spring.
Check before you go
after heavy rain.

You pass Bobadela, Cima de Vila and Padroso, and reach Xunqueira de Ambía, ~14 km in and ~21 km short of Ourense, which the Xunta calls an important spiritual centre in the Middle Ages. Soon after you cross the Roman road XVIII, the Via Nova from Braga to Astorga, where Roman milestones still stand. At Os Casares many pilgrims once turned aside to the sanctuary of Santa Mariña de Augasantas, the Xunta says. The way goes on by Paderne de Allariz, Taboadela and San Cibrao das Viñas to Ourense.

The Xunta calls Ourense a capital of thermal baths, with a famous Roman bridge and a great Romanesque cathedral. Wikipedia places the hot springs called the Burgas in the old town, and the Junta notes that Ourense is the only provincial capital in Galicia without a coast. It deserves a rest day. The Xunta gives ~35 km and the Junta ~35 km.
The character of these days

Five days take you out of the city of the Miño and over the green hills of the Deza to the cathedral. By the Xunta's stage lengths they add up to ~107 km, and by the Junta's table, from 2011, to ~111 km. The Xunta rates every one of them Medium except the last, which it rates Low.

From A Laxe, in the parish of Bendoiro, you share the road with the Camino de Invierno. The Xunta says the Winter Way joins the Vía de la Plata at Lalín, and its stage pages put the meeting at A Laxe, ~50 km from Santiago. The last two days here are the last two days of
The Winter Way
, which tells them at more length.
Day 12: Ourense to Cea (~23 km)

The stage starts at the old Roman bridge, and the Xunta gives two ways out of the city. One, by the Costiña de Canedo, follows the right bank of the Miño along the N-120. The other climbs by Cudeiro, a fine height with good views, along stretches of Camino Real with the old paving still in place. They meet again at As Casas Novas, beside the N-525.

Further on come Tamallancos and, at Sobreira, a detour to the castle-pazo of Vilamarín, then Ponte Sobreira, a handsome historic stone bridge over the River Barbantiño. San Cristovo de Cea, which the Xunta places about two kilometres from the junction, is famous for its wheat bread.
The Xunta rates the day Medium, and gives ~23 km. The Junta's table, which ends at San Cristovo de Cea, gives ~22 km.
Day 13: Cea to Dozón (~15 km)
The shortest day of the road, and a chance to choose. From the sanctuary of A Saleta the Xunta gives two options. The shorter goes by Piñor, through oak woods and lanes between oaks called
corredoiras

, to O Castro de Dozón, a small town that is the head of its municipality. The other goes by the monastery of Oseira, a Cistercian house of the twelfth century, whose community life, the Xunta says, began in 1137 and which has a long tradition of welcoming pilgrims. The Junta places Oseira ~9 km from Cea.

The Xunta describes the way to Oseira as long stretches of woodland that can be difficult at times, in complete solitude. From the monastery you come back to Dozón, and at A Gouxa, in the municipality of Dozón, you are in the province of Pontevedra. The Xunta lists ~15 km for both options, but the way by Oseira looks longer, since the Junta puts the monastery ~9 km from Cea and the road then returns to Dozón. Ask the length locally.
Day 14: Dozón to Bendoiro (~19 km)

You leave Dozón by the church for the Alto de Santo Domingo, ~736 m, which the Xunta calls cold country with frequent snow in the hardest months. The land is high, lonely and bare, with place names that recall a pre-Roman past, and then it drops fast to the River Dezón at Pontenoufe, ~8 km on, where you enter the municipality of Lalín.

You go on through small villages along a Camino Real that once had inns and still keeps something of their air. The Xunta names San Xoán de Botos as the home of the painter Laxeiro, and Donsión, whose Baroque church is a fine one. Lalín, capital of the Deza, lies ~4 km from Donsión. The day ends at Bendoiro, where A Laxe is the meeting point with the Winter Way. The Xunta gives ~19 km.
Day 15: Bendoiro to Outeiro (~34 km)

The longest day of this end of the road. The first metres follow the N-525, and then the way keeps to the Deza country by Vilasoa, Prado and the medieval bridge of Taboada over the River Deza, to Silleda, ~9 km in. Beyond lie O Foxo, Chapa and A Bandeira, ~17 km in, and the
pazo
of Santo Estevo de Oca, which the Xunta says is called the Galician Versailles for its gardens.

At A Ponte Ulla you cross the River Ulla by a historic bridge and enter the municipality of Vedra, and with it the province of A Coruña. The stage ends in Vedra, at Outeiro. The Xunta rates the day Medium and gives ~34 km. Silleda and A Bandeira are natural places to split it.
Day 16: Outeiro to Santiago (~17 km)

After Rubial a detour leads to the Pico Sacro, the Xunta says more than five hundred metres high, tied to the tradition of the bulls that the Apostle's disciples tamed to carry his body to its tomb. Then the way passes A Susana and enters Santiago by the Sar district. After the bridge over the Sar there is one last effort: a hard climb up the Rúa do Sar and the Rúa do Castrón Douro. At the top you pass under the Porta de Mazarelos, the only gate that still stands of the old medieval wall, and the last steps go by the Praza da Universidade, the Rúa da Calderería and the Praza das Praterías to the Praza do Obradoiro.
The Xunta rates the day Low and gives ~17 km. The Junta's table, which starts from Ponte Ulla, gives ~20 km.

chapters.title: Long days and other ways to split

spans.t: The sixteen days of this book follow the stage towns the sources use. They are not the only way to walk the road, and three of them are ~34 km or more. This chapter shows where each long day can be cut, and the one real choice of route. Before you count on a split, ask whether you can sleep there: that is a question for the app and for local information, and this book does not answer it.
The sixteen days at a glance

items.t: Granja de Moreruela to Tábara, ~26 km
Tábara to Santa Marta de Tera, ~23 km
Santa Marta de Tera to Rionegro del Puente, ~27 km
Rionegro del Puente to San Salvador de Palazuelo, ~19 km
San Salvador de Palazuelo to Puebla de Sanabria, ~22 km
Puebla de Sanabria to Requejo, ~12 km
Requejo to Lubián, ~19 km
Lubián to A Gudiña, ~27 km
A Gudiña to Laza, ~35 km
Laza to Vilar de Barrio, ~19 km
Vilar de Barrio to Ourense, ~35 km
Ourense to Cea, ~23 km
Cea to Dozón, ~15 km
Dozón to Bendoiro, ~19 km
Bendoiro to Outeiro, ~34 km
Outeiro to Santiago, ~17 km

spans.t: The three longest days

items.t: A Gudiña to Laza (~35 km).
Campobecerros is ~21 km in and leaves ~15 km. The Xunta rates the first two sections High.
Vilar de Barrio to Ourense (~35 km).
Xunqueira de Ambía is ~14 km in and leaves ~21 km.
Bendoiro to Outeiro (~34 km).
Silleda is ~9 km in and A Bandeira ~17 km in.

spans.t: On the Zamora days the Junta's table lists many villages between the stage towns. By that table, Faramontanos de Tábara is ~18.5 km from Granja de Moreruela, which leaves ~7.5 km to Tábara. Villar de Farfón is ~21 km beyond Santa Marta de Tera, which leaves ~6.5 km to Rionegro del Puente. Mombuey is ~8.5 km from Rionegro del Puente, on a day of ~19 km.
Days you can join

items.t: Puebla de Sanabria to Lubián in one day
is ~31 km by the Junta's table, the sum of Days 6 and 7. It crosses the Padornelo pass, so choose it only in settled weather, and keep Requejo in mind as the place to stop.
Ourense to Dozón
is ~38 km, the sum of Days 12 and 13, and would skip the option of Oseira. You may prefer to keep the short day.

spans.t: The route choice: Laza or Verín

At A Gudiña the Xunta says the road has two itineraries. One is the Verea Sur by Laza, Vilar de Barrio and Xunqueira de Ambía, which this book follows. The other, called the Itinerario de Monterrei, goes by Verín, Xinzo de Limia and Allariz, and the two meet again at Ourense.

The Xunta's stage lengths for the Verín way are ~42 km from A Gudiña to Verín, ~35 km to Xinzo de Limia, ~21 km to Allariz and ~23 km to Ourense. That is ~120 km, against ~89 km by Laza, so ~31 km longer, and the Xunta's own totals differ by the same amount: ~253 km against ~222 km.

You trade the high country of the Verea Sur for a longer road through valleys and the plain of A Limia. The Xunta mentions the great castle of Monterrei, whose outline shows on the skyline as you near Verín, the former lake of A Limia, the Lagoa de Antela, once the largest freshwater lake in Spain and drained in the 1960s, and Allariz, which it calls one of the most beautiful and best preserved towns in Galicia. The Junta's guide lists pilgrims' hospitals in Verín and Monterrei. The Xunta also says the way from A Gudiña to Verín stays close to the N-525 and the A-52 motorway.
Roads that join

The Xunta says that old Portuguese roads from the interior enter Ourense province along its whole southern border and join the Vía de la Plata at Verín, Laza, Xinzo and Ourense. The one from Chaves, by Feces, reaches Laza, where it joins the Verea Sur. The Confraternity of St James describes a road from Zamora by Bragança in Portugal that reaches the Camino Sanabrés at Verín. If you arrive from one of those roads, you will share the last days with this one.
Starting later
If your time is short, the sums are these.

items.t: From Puebla de Sanabria, ~255 km by the Junta's table.
From Lubián, ~224 km by the Junta's table, and ~222 km by the Xunta's.
From A Gudiña, ~196 km by the Xunta's lengths, and ~201 km by the Junta's table.
From Ourense, ~107 km by the Xunta's lengths, and ~111 km by the Junta's table.

spans.t: The chapter on arriving says what the Pilgrim's Office writes about the last hundred kilometres. Rest days are in the chapter on sleeping, eating and resting.
Where you will sleep
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: shared rooms, bunk beds, a shared bathroom and sometimes a kitchen, and a
hospitalero
, the host, who stamps your credencial. The Pilgrim's Office says the credencial gives access to the hostels of the Way, so keep it with you.

In Galicia the Xunta runs a public network of hostels, begun in 1993. Its rules, as it states them now, matter on a quiet road. Places are filled as pilgrims arrive, and no reservation is taken. The stay is one night. Priority goes first to pilgrims with physical limitations, then to those on foot, then on horseback, then by bicycle, and last to people travelling with a support car. Rules change, so read the Xunta's page before you go.

The Office adds that hostels with no subsidy are kept going, in austerity, by pilgrims' contributions, so leave what you can and leave the place clean. It also asks groups travelling with a support car, or by bicycle, to find other shelter than the pilgrim hostels.

This book names no hostel and says where none is. Hostels open and close, and a wrong line costs a tired person dearly. In Zamora the villages are small, some with a dozen people. The Junta's guide of 2010 says the road has hostels and services enough to be entirely workable, while the Confraternity of St James asks for extra care in planning. So work out your nights first, then your days, and confirm the night before.
Living with other people

items.t: Be quiet early and late.
Pack your bag the night before, and use a torch, not the ceiling light, when you leave in the dark.
Keep your boots and pack off the beds.
Some hostels ask for boots to be left at the door, so ask.
Check your bunk before you unpack.
If you find bites or bugs, tell the
hospitalero
, and if you can, wash and dry your clothes on a hot cycle.
Earplugs and a sleep mask
are the usual answer to snoring and early lights.

spans.t: Eating
A
menú del peregrino
is a set meal for pilgrims, offered in some places. This book gives no prices and names no restaurant: ask where you sleep.

The sources describe food that belongs to the country. Wikipedia says Zamora is known for pulses, sheep's-milk cheese and the honey of Sanabria. The Junta's guide names home-cooked stews of veal, lamb, kid and chicken around Tábara, and for Sanabria its beans, its mountain beef and an octopus dish. It describes the
magosto

, the chestnut feast, with chestnuts roasted, boiled with milk or bathed in honey. The Xunta says San Cristovo de Cea is famous for its wheat bread, and the Junta that the monks of Oseira make cheese, honey and liqueurs.

The practical point is the gaps. Buy lunch the day before, fill your bottles at every village, and do not trust a village on the map to have anything open when you arrive. On the high Verea Sur, the Xunta says, the villages are half abandoned.
Rest days

A rest day is part of a plan, not a failure of it. Puebla de Sanabria comes at the end of the fifth day, with its castle, its old streets and the lake nearby, and Ourense at the end of the eleventh, with its hot springs. Santiago comes last. The chapter on arriving says why to stay a second day there.
In the evening
Wash your feet and look at them before you sleep. Then spend ten minutes on tomorrow: how long it is, where you will eat lunch, where the water is, and where you will sleep.
This chapter is plain on purpose. On a road with few people and long gaps, a small mistake costs more than it does on a busy one.
Heat

The Zamora plain and the city of Ourense are the hot parts of the road. The mean daily high is ~31 °C in July at both, and Wikipedia's tables give records of ~42 °C at Zamora and ~44 °C at Ourense. The Confraternity of St James says summer temperatures on the Vía de la Plata can pass 40 degrees and should be avoided.

items.t: Walk at first light, and plan to finish by early afternoon.
Carry water for the whole stage. The Xunta asks for about two litres a day, and in heat you will need more.
Wear a hat and sun cream, and rest in the shade in the hottest hours.
If you feel faint, dizzy or confused, stop in the shade, drink, and get help. Call 112 if it does not pass.

spans.t: Cold, fog and the high ground

The road climbs to ~1,260 m at Padornelo, and the Xunta puts the pass of Portela da Canda at ~1,262 m. It describes the Serra Seca as landscape above a thousand metres, and says the Alto de Santo Domingo, at only ~736 m, has frequent snow in the hardest months. The Junta's guide says that in the last villages of Castilla y León and across Galicia the temperature can fall, with fog and the risk of rain, in any season.

items.t: Read the AEMET warnings for the area the evening before, and again at breakfast.
Carry a warm layer and a waterproof even in summer.
Do not cross a high pass in poor visibility. Choose where you will stop before you set out, for example Requejo before the Padornelo pass, or Campobecerros on the Serra Seca.
In winter, ask locally about snow and ice before you commit to a mountain day.

spans.t: Rain and water on the path

Galicia is wet. By Wikipedia's tables Ourense receives ~108 to ~119 mm a month from October to December, and Santiago ~184 to ~214 mm. The Xunta says that between Vilar de Barrio and Ourense some stretches of the Verea de Santiago are sometimes flooded in winter and spring. The Confraternity warns of high water and muddy tracks after heavy rain on the Vía de la Plata.
Check before you go
, and after heavy rain ask where you slept.
Roads and traffic

The Way runs beside the national road N-525 and crosses the A-52 motorway. Where there is no verge, stay where drivers can see you and you can see them, and keep your ears free of earphones. The Xunta advises against walking in the dark, before dawn or after sunset.
Being alone

The quiet that the sources praise in this road is also its risk. The Xunta describes stretches of half-abandoned villages, and a way through woodland that can be difficult, taken in complete solitude.

items.t: Tell your host where you are going, and when you expect to arrive.
Carry food and water for the whole stage, and a charged phone, but do not count on a signal in the mountains.
Ring ahead if you will be late.

spans.t: Feet and body

The Xunta says that knees, tendons and feet are the weak points, and that sprains and tendinitis are the commonest injuries. Wear boots you have already walked in, change your socks, wash your feet at the end of the day, and look at them. Treat a hot spot before it becomes a blister. Eat light, with plenty of carbohydrate, and drink before, during and after the walk.
When to stop

Stopping early is a plan, not a failure. If you are hurt, ill or lost, or the weather turns, stop. Anything that worries you is a reason to see a doctor, and this book gives no medical advice beyond that. The European emergency number is 112. The Xunta says it is free, works every hour of every day, and answers any urgent call. The Xunta's portal also offers a guide to emergencies for pilgrims as a PDF.
Many reasons, an old road

People walk to Santiago for faith, for sport, for grief, out of curiosity, or to rest from work. All of those reasons are welcome on this road, and it has always had more than one kind of traveller. The Xunta says that A Mezquita, where the road enters Galicia, was a land crossed by pilgrims, but also by reapers, muleteers, dealers and travellers who came for many different reasons. The Junta's guide says the road began as a link between two kingdoms, and that pilgrims came to use it afterwards. You will be walking in the steps of people who had every sort of errand.

The Zamora tourism board says that at Granja de Moreruela the pilgrimage to Santiago "begins, or rather continues", for most walkers. Some of you will arrive with weeks of the Vía de la Plata behind you, and some will start with a clean credencial. Both are at home here.
What a quiet road gives you

A road with few people leaves long hours with nothing to do but walk. You may find that this is welcome, or that it is hard, or that it is both on the same day. There is no right answer. The Zamora plain gives you distance, and a horizon to rest your eyes on. The mountains give you effort and a reason to go slowly. The last days, among the oaks and small bridges of the Deza, give you, after A Laxe, the company of the Winter Way.

The Junta's guide reports an inscription in Valdemerilla, a village with twelve inhabitants. In translation it says that the village embodies calm and makes everything relative, and that few people here are a crowd. You do not need to walk to a village to try that thought. You can try it at the next bench.
Questions for the walk
Carry one of these for an hour, and let it go if it does not help.

items.t: What are you carrying that you could leave behind?
When did you last go a whole morning without speaking?
What is the first thing you notice when the road is empty?
What would you say to the person you most wish were walking beside you?
What does enough look like for you today: enough kilometres, enough water, enough rest?
What are you walking towards, and what are you walking away from? Are they the same thing?

spans.t: In the evening
Write three lines, or none. What did you see? What did your body say? What do you need tomorrow? If you pray, this is a good hour for it. If you do not, this is a good hour for being still.
The last streets

The last streets are the ones the Xunta describes: over the River Sar, up the Rúa do Sar and the Rúa do Castrón Douro, through the Porta de Mazarelos, to the Praza do Obradoiro. Wikipedia says that construction of the present cathedral began in 1075 and that it was consecrated in 1211. It is a Romanesque church with Gothic and Baroque additions, built over the reputed tomb of St James. The Baroque façade on the Obradoiro square was completed in 1740, and behind it stands the Romanesque Pórtico da Gloria of Master Mateo, whose completion in 1188 was carved on a stone. The crypt below the high altar is where pilgrims of the ninth-century church ended their journey.
Pilgrims' Masses are held in the cathedral, and their times change, so ask on the day. The
botafumeiro

, the great swinging censer, is used on certain important religious holidays and, Wikipedia says, at all Pilgrims' Masses in a Holy Year. 2027 is a Holy Year, and the Holy Door is opened only in Holy Years.
The Compostela

The Compostela is the certificate that the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules. The Office owns the rules, and they can change. This book says what the Office says, and sends you to the Office in any doubt.

items.t: The Office gives it to pilgrims who follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback, with the credencial stamped along the route.
It asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle.

On foot or on horseback, that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the cathedral.

You may walk the Way in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and at the end of each stage, with the date.
A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain.
The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

spans.t: The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

On its own pages the Office says the Certificate of Distance records the day and the starting point of your pilgrimage, the kilometres you covered, the day you arrived and the route, and that someone who has walked before can request it.
This road and the rule

From Granja de Moreruela you have ~370 km ahead of you, far more than the last hundred kilometres the Office asks for. A start further on is a matter of arithmetic, and the arithmetic here is close in one place.

items.t: From Ourense, the Xunta's stage lengths add up to ~107 km, and the Junta's table says ~111 km. That is near the limit, and a detour, or a different way of measuring, changes the answer.
From Cea, the Xunta's lengths add up to ~84 km, which is short of the hundred kilometres the Office writes.
From A Gudiña, the same lengths add up to ~196 km, far more than the minimum.

If you came by the Winter Way, which joins this road at A Laxe, ~50 km from Santiago, note that the Office's rule speaks of the same route. This book does not say how the Office counts a walk that begins on one route and ends on another.

spans.t: This book does not say whether any particular start counts. Ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go, say where you plan to start, and keep your credencial stamped along the way. The Office's pages on the Compostela, the credencial and the Certificate of Distance do not name the routes it recognises.
At the Pilgrim's Office

The Office issues the Compostela, a document in Latin. You will need your stamped credencial. Procedures and hours change, so look at the Office's own website before you arrive, and do not plan a tight connection for the same day.
Whatever the Compostela means to you, it is a record of a road you walked, not a measure of it.
The next day
Do not leave on the morning after you arrive. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it rewards a second day.

items.t: Rest.
After ~370 km your legs have earned it.
See the cathedral without a queue behind you.
Sit in the Obradoiro square and watch the others arrive.
Think about what comes next.
If you want to keep walking, the Camino to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km, goes on from Santiago, and has its own book in this series.
Plan your way home
with the timetables in front of you, not at the last minute.

spans.t: The Way does not end at the cathedral. It may end a few days later, in a kitchen, when you notice that you no longer hurry through a meal.
The first week

Give yourself time. You may find the return harder than the road, and the reason is not hard to see: for days on end your whole job was to walk, eat, wash and sleep. Your body may want to keep walking. Let it. Take a short walk each day, even if it is only round the block, and eat something simple.
Look at your credencial. Each stamp marks a night and a door that opened. Keep it somewhere you will see it.
Keeping the road

items.t: Write it down while you remember it.
Three lines a day is enough. The names of the villages go first.
Send a note to someone who gave you a bed.
A line of thanks costs little.
Walk again, on a smaller scale.
A local path, a spare Saturday and a flask of tea keep the habit alive.
Keep the questions.
Pick one from the chapter on the inner Way and carry it for a week at home.

spans.t: Walking again

If this was your first Camino, the others have their own books in this series. If you walked in from the Vía de la Plata, you already know what a long road does to a person. If you walked only the end, the beginning is still there, on the plain of Zamora, and you can walk it another year.
Buen Camino
, and welcome home.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus

. The app is still in development. The Camino Sanabrés is on its list of routes, from Granja de Moreruela to Santiago de Compostela, and the app gives it no distance and no number of stages. This book makes no claim about what the app holds for it today, so look in the app, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and its fact ledger lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Xunta de Galicia

, on its official Camino de Santiago portal (caminodesantiago.gal): the page on the Vía de la Plata or Camino Mozárabe, in English and Spanish, and the stage pages for the way by Laza and the way by Verín in Spanish, with their sections, lengths, ratings and descriptions; and the portal's pages on advice for pilgrims, on physical and mental preparation and on the public network of hostels. The Xunta's page on the Camino de Invierno confirms where that road joins.
The Junta de Castilla y León
, on its tourism site (turismocastillayleon.com): the chapter on the Camino Mozárabe-Sanabrés in its guide to the historic Caminos, in an edition of 2010 with data updated in February 2011.
The Diputación de Zamora
, Patronato de Turismo: its leaflet on the Camino Sanabrés, of March 2010.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Vía de la Plata, which takes in the Camino Sanabrés, updated in August 2025.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the pages on the Compostela, the credencial, the Certificate of Distance, planning and the history of the pilgrimage.
Wikipedia

, for geography, climate tables and history: the articles on Granja de Moreruela, Zamora, Puebla de Sanabria, Ourense, Santiago de Compostela, its cathedral and airport, the Jacobean Holy Year and the Camino de Santiago route descriptions.
A standard solar calculation
, for the hours of daylight.
The CaminoPlus route catalog, website and route guide
, for the route's start and end, the website's ~370 km and its 15 to 17 stages, the difficulty rating and the app's own note.

spans.t: The Junta's guide and the Zamora leaflet are from 2010 and 2011. Churches and landscape change slowly, but waymarks, surfaces and services may have changed. The Xunta's English pages can be machine-translated from Spanish, so this book follows the Spanish originals.

Published figures differ between these sources, so every distance in this book is marked ~. Where the sources say nothing, the book says nothing and tells you to check. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the villages who point the way and say
Buen Camino
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims.
Cabildo
: the governing council of the cathedral.
Cofradía
: a brotherhood, such as the one at Rionegro del Puente.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Corredoira
: a sunken lane between walls or trees, in Galician.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Junta
: the regional government of Castilla y León.
Magosto
: the autumn feast of chestnuts.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Pazo
: a Galician manor house.
Sello
: a stamp in the credencial.
Venda
: a roadside inn, from which several place names on the Serra Seca take their name.
Xunta
: the regional government of Galicia.
